title: Introduction to the Epistles to the Thessalonians
subtitle: A concise guide to the authorship, setting, occasion, and purposes of the two letters Paul sent to a young and persecuted church in Macedonia.

blocks.text: Both letters open in the same way: Paul, Silvanus, and Timothy send greetings to the Thessalonian congregation, a church that lives in God the Father and in the Lord Jesus Christ. The three names reflect a real partnership, since all three men had preached in the city together, and the frequent use of we throughout the letters keeps that fellowship in view. Yet the voice that breaks through again and again is Paul’s own. He speaks in the first person of his longing to return, of being hindered by Satan, and of sending Timothy when he could bear the silence no longer, and he closes the second letter with a greeting written in his own hand.

The first letter has enjoyed almost unbroken acceptance as Paul’s work. Its warmth toward new converts, its threefold pattern of faith, love, and hope, its gospel of the death and resurrection of Jesus, and its personal recollections of the founding visit all bear his stamp. The early churches received it among his letters, it appears in the oldest lists of New Testament books, and Christian writers of the second century drew on its language about the trumpet and the Lord’s descent. Apart from a few passing challenges that quickly faded, it has been treated as genuine from the beginning, and it stands as one of the clearest windows into the apostle’s pastoral heart.

Second Thessalonians was likewise received without hesitation in the ancient church. It stood beside the first letter in the earliest collections, and writers in the second century show familiarity with its teaching about the man of sin and the patience of the saints. Only in the modern period were doubts raised. Some readers judged its prophetic section unlike anything else in Paul, others felt that its tone was cooler than the first letter, and still others argued that its close resemblance to 1 Thessalonians looked like the work of an imitator copying a model rather than an apostle writing freely.

These objections are weaker than they first appear. Paul received visions and revelations, and his other letters show that he could speak of the end in vivid prophetic terms when a church needed it. A changed tone is natural when a pastor must correct a dangerous error and confront members who refuse to work. The similarity of wording is just what one would expect if the same writer addressed the same congregation on related questions within a few months. The two letters do not contradict each other: one stresses that the day will come suddenly on the unprepared, the other that certain events must precede it, and Jesus Himself held both truths together in His teaching on the Mount of Olives.

The letter also bears marks that a later forger would have found hard to invent. It assumes a living congregation suffering present persecution, it refers to oral teaching Paul gave while still with them, and it warns against letters falsely claiming his authority, a strange thing for an imitator to write. Its closing signature in Paul’s own hand, offered as a mark in every letter, points to an apostle anxious to protect his readers from deception. Taken together, the internal character and the steady witness of the early church give strong reason to receive both letters as the authentic writing of the apostle Paul.

The letters can be dated with unusual precision for an ancient document. Acts places the founding of the church on Paul’s second missionary journey, after the Jerusalem Council and the preaching at Philippi. From Thessalonica Paul moved to Berea, then to Athens, and finally to Corinth, where he stayed a year and a half. During that stay he was brought before Gallio, the proconsul of Achaia. An inscription found at Delphi allows Gallio’s term to be placed around A.D. 51 to 52, which fixes Paul’s Corinthian ministry within a narrow window of time and anchors the whole sequence of events.

First Thessalonians was written soon after Timothy came back from Macedonia with news of the church. Paul says that he had been left alone at Athens and had sent Timothy to strengthen the believers, and Acts records that Silas and Timothy rejoined him at Corinth. Some ancient copies carry a closing note naming Athens as the place of writing, but that guess was probably drawn from the mention of Athens in chapter 3. Since the letter speaks of Timothy’s return as already past, Corinth is the more natural setting, early in Paul’s stay there, around A.D. 50 or 51.

The second letter followed within a few months. The same three names stand in its greeting, and nothing indicates that Silas worked with Paul after the Corinthian period, so the setting is almost certainly still Corinth. The church’s situation has developed, but not changed beyond recognition: persecution continues, confusion about the day of the Lord has grown, and the idle members warned in the first letter have not mended their ways. A date around A.D. 51 fits these details well. These two letters are therefore among the earliest writings of the New Testament, and quite possibly the first of Paul’s letters to survive.

Some have suggested that 2 Thessalonians was actually written first, pointing to its emphasis on present persecution and its brief treatment of matters the other letter handles more fully. The traditional order remains far more likely. The second letter speaks of an earlier letter from Paul, it builds on teaching about the Lord’s coming already given, and its correction of excitement about the day of the Lord makes best sense after the strong emphasis on the Advent in the first letter had been misread. The early date matters, for it shows that within two decades of the cross the resurrection of Jesus, His return, and holy living were already the settled faith of a Gentile church.

Thessalonica was founded around 316 B.C. by Cassander, one of the generals who divided the empire of Alexander the Great, and was named after his wife, a half sister of Alexander. It stood at the head of the Thermaic Gulf with a fine natural harbor, and it quickly became one of the leading ports of the northern Aegean. When Rome organized Macedonia as a province in the second century B.C., Thessalonica became the seat of the governor. In Paul’s day it was the largest and most influential city of the province, home to a mixed population of Greeks, Romans, Jews, and traders from around the eastern Mediterranean.

The city’s importance owed much to the Via Egnatia, the great Roman highway that ran across the Balkan peninsula from the Adriatic coast to Byzantium. Soldiers, officials, merchants, and travelers passed through constantly, and news moved quickly along the road and through the harbor. This explains how the faith of the young church could sound out not only in Macedonia and Achaia but in every place. A congregation planted at such a crossroads was ideally placed to become a center from which the gospel spread to the towns and regions round about.

Thessalonica held the privileged status of a free city, granted by Rome as a reward for loyalty during the civil wars of the first century B.C. It governed its own local affairs through a council and a board of magistrates called politarchs, minted its own coins, and was spared a Roman garrison within its walls. Luke’s use of this precise title for the city officials, a term now confirmed by inscriptions found in the region, reflects his careful knowledge of local detail. Such a city had every reason to guard its good standing with Rome and to treat any hint of disloyalty with alarm.

Religious life was crowded and varied. Inscriptions and coins point to the worship of many gods, among them Dionysus, the Egyptian deities Serapis and Isis, and Cabirus, a local patron deity. Alongside these the city paid honor to Roma and to Roman benefactors, and a temple was raised to Julius Caesar, whose adopted son Augustus also received divine honors on the city’s coinage. Loyalty to the emperor and devotion to the gods were woven into the city’s festivals, trade guilds, and public life. Converts who turned from idols to serve the living and true God therefore stepped away from far more than private habits; they withdrew from the shared religious life that held their city together.

The language of Paul’s letters would have carried a sharp edge in this setting. Words such as coming, appearing, peace and safety, Lord, and gospel were already in use for the visits of rulers and the blessings of imperial rule. When Paul proclaimed another King, Jesus, whose coming would bring sudden destruction on those who trusted in a false peace, his message could easily sound like a challenge to Caesar. That background helps explain the charge brought before the politarchs and the steady pressure that followed the believers after Paul left.

sections.title: The Founding and Makeup of the Church

blocks.text: Following his usual practice, Paul began in the synagogue. For three Sabbaths he reasoned with the Jews from the Scriptures, explaining and demonstrating that the Messiah had to suffer and rise from the dead, and that this Messiah was Jesus. Some of the Jews were persuaded, along with a great number of God-fearing Greeks and not a few of the leading women of the city. The gospel came, Paul later reminded them, not in word only but in power, in the Holy Spirit, and with full assurance, and the hearers received it as the word of God rather than a merely human message.

The letters show that the congregation was largely Gentile. Paul speaks of them turning to God from idols, a description that would hardly fit converts from the synagogue, and he warns them not to live in passionate lust like the Gentiles who do not know God. Many of them seem to have been working people. Paul urges them to work with their own hands, and he himself labored night and day at his trade so as not to burden anyone. The household of Jason, who welcomed the missionaries, may have served as an early meeting place, and names such as Aristarchus and Secundus later appear among Paul’s companions.

The stay was longer than three weeks. Paul received gifts from Philippi more than once while he was in Thessalonica, and the letters describe a period of work, teaching, and close fellowship in which he dealt with them as a father with his children. Even so, the time was short. Paul had to leave before he could teach them all he wished, and he speaks of longing to supply what was lacking in their faith. A young church with little formal instruction, surrounded by idolatry and facing hostility, needed the steadying word that the letters would provide.

Opposition came quickly. Some of the synagogue leaders, moved by jealousy, gathered a crowd from the marketplace, set the city in an uproar, and attacked Jason’s house. Unable to find Paul and Silas, they dragged Jason and some believers before the politarchs, charging that these men who had turned the world upside down were acting against the decrees of Caesar by saying there was another king. The magistrates took security from Jason and released them, but the missionaries were sent away by night. The believers who remained inherited the suspicion of their neighbors, and their suffering became the backdrop of both letters.

The story of Paul’s dealings with the church can be traced from Acts and from the letters themselves. It moves from the vision at Troas that called the missionaries into Europe, through the hurried departure from Thessalonica, to the anxious waiting in Athens and the joyful news that reached Paul in Corinth. Each stage left its mark on the letters, which often look back to what happened during the founding visit and in the months that followed.

blocks.title: Paul and the Thessalonian Church
blocks.note: Dates are approximate and follow the sequence of Acts 16–18 and the letters themselves.

events.title: Called into Macedonia
events.description: At Troas Paul sees a vision of a man of Macedonia and crosses into Europe with Silas, Timothy, and Luke.

events.title: Suffering at Philippi
events.description: Paul and Silas are beaten and imprisoned at Philippi, then released and asked to leave the city.

events.title: Preaching in Thessalonica
events.description: Paul reasons in the synagogue for three Sabbaths, a church is gathered, and he works night and day among them.

events.title: Uproar and Departure
events.description: A mob attacks Jason’s house, the politarchs take security, and the missionaries are sent away by night to Berea.

events.title: Waiting in Athens
events.description: Driven from Berea, Paul goes to Athens and sends Timothy back to strengthen the Thessalonian believers.

events.title: 1 Thessalonians from Corinth
events.description: Timothy returns with good news of their faith and love, and Paul writes to encourage and instruct them.

events.title: 2 Thessalonians from Corinth
events.description: Hearing of confusion about the day of the Lord and of idle members, Paul writes again to correct and steady them.

blocks.text: Paul’s separation from the church was painful to him. He describes himself as torn away from them like an orphan, and he says that he tried more than once to return, but Satan hindered him. Unable to go himself, he chose to be left alone at Athens and sent Timothy, his trusted coworker, to establish them and to learn whether the tempter had undone their labor. The letter shows that Paul’s concern was not for his own reputation alone but for their standing in the faith under pressure.

Timothy’s report brought Paul great relief. The believers were holding fast in faith and love, they remembered their teachers kindly, and they longed to see Paul as much as he longed to see them. In his own affliction at Corinth, the news made him feel alive again. Yet the report also revealed needs: grief over members who had died, questions about the coming of the Lord, pressure toward the sexual standards of the surrounding culture, and some who were neglecting daily work. The first letter answers these with thanksgiving, explanation, and loving exhortation.

Paul later revisited Macedonia on his third journey and passed through the region again on his way to Jerusalem, and Thessalonian believers such as Aristarchus became his companions in travel and even in imprisonment. The church that began in turmoil became a lasting partner in the gospel. Its story shows how God used a brief and interrupted mission, carried on by letters and messengers, to build a congregation that would stand through affliction.

The first purpose of the letter is thanksgiving and encouragement. Paul remembers before God their work of faith, labor of love, and patience of hope in the Lord Jesus Christ. He rejoices that they received the word in much affliction with joy of the Holy Spirit and became examples to believers throughout Macedonia and Achaia. Nearly half of the letter is devoted to recalling the founding visit and the bond between apostle and church, so that suffering believers would know that their faith was real and that God had chosen and called them.

A second purpose was to defend the integrity of the missionaries. After Paul’s sudden departure, opponents may have suggested that he was another wandering speaker seeking money or glory who abandoned his followers when trouble came. Paul answers by reminding them how he and his companions conducted themselves: they came with boldness after suffering at Philippi, spoke to please God rather than people, refused flattery and greed, worked to support themselves, and cared for the believers as a nursing mother and a father. His absence was not neglect but enforced separation, and his sending of Timothy proved his love.

Paul also wrote to strengthen their holiness. He urges them to abstain from sexual immorality, to control their bodies in purity and honor, and to remember that God has called them not to uncleanness but to holiness. He commends their love for one another and encourages them to grow in it further, while also calling them to live quietly, mind their own affairs, and work with their hands, so that they would walk honestly toward outsiders and lack nothing. Practical godliness runs through the whole letter, rooted in the grace that called them.

The best-known purpose concerns those who had died. Some believers were grieving as if their loved ones had lost all share in the Lord’s coming. Paul answers that the dead in Christ are asleep, resting unconscious in the grave until the resurrection, not living on in some other place. When the Lord Himself descends from heaven with a shout, with the voice of the archangel, and with the trumpet of God, the dead in Christ will rise first, and the living will be caught up together with them to meet the Lord. The coming he describes is personal, visible, and audible, with nothing secret about it, and it brings the whole church together into the Lord’s presence.

Finally, Paul prepares the church to live in readiness. The day of the Lord will come as a thief in the night, unexpected and sudden for those who say peace and safety, but believers are children of the light and need not be overtaken. They are to keep awake, be sober, and put on faith, love, and the hope of salvation. The closing exhortations call for respect toward leaders, patience with all, care for the fainthearted and weak, joyful prayer and thanksgiving, and careful testing of all things, as Paul prays that God will sanctify them completely and keep them blameless at the coming of Jesus Christ.

The second letter begins, like the first, with thanksgiving, but its immediate concern is encouragement under mounting persecution. Paul thanks God that their faith is growing exceedingly and their love abounding, and he boasts of their patience in all their afflictions. He assures them that their suffering is evidence of God’s righteous judgment, which will count them worthy of His kingdom. When the Lord Jesus is revealed from heaven with His mighty angels in flaming fire, He will give rest to His afflicted people and repay those who trouble them. The punishment of the disobedient is everlasting destruction, a final ruin away from the presence of the Lord, rather than a life of endless suffering.

The central reason for the letter was a dangerous error about the day of the Lord. Someone had unsettled the church by claiming that the day had already come, whether through a supposed spirit utterance, a spoken word, or a letter falsely claiming to be from Paul. Some believers were shaken and alarmed. It seems that the first letter’s strong emphasis on the nearness and suddenness of the Advent had been pressed into a feverish expectation that the end was immediately at hand, and agitators were taking advantage of the fainthearted.

Paul answers that the day will not come until the falling away comes first and the man of sin is revealed. He reminds them that he had already taught them these things in person. The falling away is an apostasy arising within the professing church, and the man of sin is the power that grows out of it, exalting itself above all that is called God and sitting in the temple of God as though it were divine. Read alongside the little horn of Daniel 7 and the beast of Revelation 13, this prophecy finds its historical fulfillment in the papal system, which developed after the restraining hand of imperial Rome was removed. The prophecy concerns a system and its claims, not the sincere believers who have lived within that communion, and it ends with that power destroyed by the brightness of Christ’s coming.

A further purpose was to deal firmly with the disorderly. The idle members whom Paul had gently warned in the first letter were still refusing to work, living off the generosity of others and busying themselves in other people’s affairs. Paul now commands them in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ to work quietly and eat their own bread. He reminds the church of his own example of toil, sets down the rule that anyone unwilling to work should not eat, and directs the congregation to withdraw from those who persist, yet without treating them as enemies but admonishing them as brothers.

Through all of this Paul seeks to establish the church in steady faith. He gives thanks that God chose them for salvation through sanctification of the Spirit and belief of the truth, urges them to stand fast and hold the teaching they had received, and prays that the Lord would comfort their hearts and establish them in every good word and work. The letter closes with a prayer for peace and with Paul’s own signature, guarding the believers against deception and directing their hearts into the love of God and the patience of Christ.

The two letters belong together as successive chapters in one pastoral relationship. Both were written from Corinth by the same three missionaries to the same young church within a short span of time. The first letter responds to Timothy’s report with relief, thanksgiving, and instruction on holy living, the hope of the resurrection, and readiness for the day of the Lord. The second responds to a later report showing that persecution had intensified and that teaching about the Advent had been twisted, and it brings comfort, correction, and firm discipline.

Their teaching about the end is complementary rather than contradictory. The first letter stresses that the coming of Christ will be sudden for the unprepared and glorious for His people, uniting the living with the raised dead in Christ. The second adds that the day will be preceded by a falling away and the revelation of the man of sin, so that believers will not be deceived by claims that it has already come. Together they guard against two opposite dangers: careless unreadiness on one side and feverish speculation on the other. Both call for sober, faithful, working lives lived in the light of His appearing.

blocks.title: Book at a Glance
rows: Author
The apostle Paul, writing with Silvanus and Timothy
Dates
1 Thessalonians: about A.D. 50–51; 2 Thessalonians: a few months later, about A.D. 51
Place of writing
Corinth, during Paul’s year and a half there on his second missionary journey
Original readers
A young, largely Gentile church in Thessalonica, the chief city of Macedonia
Setting
A church founded amid opposition, left early by its teachers, and facing continuing persecution
1 Thessalonians
Thanksgiving for faith, defense of the mission, a call to holiness, and comfort about the dead in Christ
2 Thessalonians
Encouragement under persecution, correction about the day of the Lord, and discipline for the idle
Central message
Those who have turned to God from idols wait for His Son from heaven and live holy, faithful lives until He comes
Representative passages

blocks.title: The Two Letters Compared
rows: Occasion
Timothy’s encouraging report after Paul’s forced departure
News of deepening persecution and confusion about the day of the Lord
Main concern
Grief over believers who had fallen asleep
Claims that the day of the Lord had already come
Teaching on the end
The Lord descends, the dead in Christ rise, and the day comes suddenly
The falling away and the man of sin come first, then Christ destroys that power
The idle members
Gentle counsel to work quietly with their own hands
Firm command to work and to withdraw from the disorderly
Pastoral tone
Warm thanksgiving and parental affection
Steadying comfort joined with authoritative correction

blocks.text: Read together, the letters show a church learning to live between conversion and consummation. Having abandoned idols, they now serve the true and living God while they await the return of His Son. That waiting is never idle. It produces faith that works, love that labors, and hope that endures, and it sets the believer’s whole life, spirit, soul, and body, under the sanctifying grace of God. The God who called them is faithful, and He will do it.
